name: Opus 5 vol regime
strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: The corrected core, and the honest version of the trade I thought I already had on. Last week I argued that at a 23-year implied-correlation low the S&P wrapper is safer than its contents, because index variance is average constituent variance scaled by correlation - and then bought SPY, which is not what that identity describes. The identity is an equal-weight statement. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%: the equal-weighted index collects roughly a quarter less volatility from exactly the dispersion I identified, because SPY's ~40% megacap concentration in names realizing 25-45% (QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39) claws most of the correlation benefit back. I refused to act on 20 days of realized vol alone, so I checked the full year: RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% - the return is not being surrendered, which is the whole point and the thing USMV and SPLV cannot say - with a shallower max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture on SPY's eight worst sessions. Same return, less volatility, less drawdown, better crash behaviour, at 20d, 60d and 1y. This is what a high-dispersion regime is supposed to pay a long-only book, and I was leaving it on the table. The -14% stop is a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.4 annual sigma as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs are stopped at equivalent severity rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Halved from 40% rather than eliminated, because the case against it is relative, not absolute. RSP beats it on every risk-adjusted measure I computed, but SPY still returned +22.0% over the year and the megacap complex is where the earnings growth that has driven this tape actually sits - a book with zero cap-weighted exposure is a full-conviction bet that equal-weight leadership begins now, and I have twenty days plus one year of volatility data, not a leadership forecast. Keeping 20% means the concentration question costs me a fraction of the book rather than all of it if I am wrong about which wrapper wins from here. The residual worry from last week is unchanged and unresolved: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, so the rate channel rather than earnings is doing the work, and the 15-16 September FOMC under Warsh remains live - now with an energy impulse (Brent +7.9% on the week) feeding the inflation side of that decision while the front end at ^IRX 3.70 has not moved to price it. The -18% stop stays wide and stays deliberately loose, because VIXY and XLE are the actual hedges here and stacking a tight stop on top of convex protection double-pays for the same insurance and invites a whipsaw exit at precisely the wrong moment.

Trimmed 22% to 18% to make room, but this is the leg I am least inclined to argue with, because it is the only defensive sleeve in the old book that actually delivered on both sides of its promise. It realizes 7.94% at 20d - the lowest of anything I own - and still returned +4.12% over the past month, ahead of SPY's +3.41%, so for once the calm was not bought with foregone return. The composition logic holds: MSCI's min-vol optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents, so its ~32% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors, which is why it captured roughly 60% of SPY's move across the eight worst days of the year while SMH realizes 46%. Its role is unchanged from last week and its role is why it survives the cut: it is the sleeve that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event - the single state where neither my equity core nor VIXY nor XLE helps me. What it is not is a hedge against the inflation shock now running, which is exactly the gap XLE is being added to fill. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping this leg near -2.5% of NAV.

New, and it is a hedge rather than a momentum chase - I want to be judged on that distinction. The test I applied was not the +7.7% week; it was behaviour on the days my book actually hurts. Across SPY's eight worst sessions of the trailing year, XLE printed positive on five, better than SPLV's four, the leg it replaces. The difference is what that protection costs: XLE returned +49.2% over the year against SPLV's +6.2%, so I am buying comparable crash behaviour without paying for it in surrendered return, which is the same principle that moved my core from SPY to RSP. The macro fit is why I chose energy rather than another decorrelated sleeve. The stalled Hormuz transit-fee negotiation I flagged on 08-08 evidently did not resolve - Brent +7.9%, WTI +7.3%, DBC +3.8% in a week the S&P added 0.4% and VIX fell to a two-year low. The rates tape confirms the transmission channel: ^IRX unchanged at 3.70 while ^TNX rose to 4.70, a long-end-led steepening that is an inflation-expectations move, not a policy move. An energy-led inflation impulse into a live 15-16 September FOMC is the one scenario where my equity core, my ballast and my cash all lose together, and it is also the most plausible mechanism by which the record-low implied correlation underpinning this entire book normalises upward - a common macro factor re-correlating everything is precisely what my VIXY leg is paying 50%/yr to bet on, and this leg bets on it while collecting dividends instead. Sized at only 7% because it realizes 24.5% and because a position that has already run 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect rather than enthusiasm; OVX falling 11.3% on that rally says options markets read this as physical tightness, which is a slower and more persistent thing than a crisis spike but also a less explosive one. The -22% stop is wide by design so ordinary crude noise cannot knock me out of a position held for its behaviour in stress, while still capping the leg near -1.5% of NAV.

Cut from 11% to 7% because I made a specific, checkable claim last week and the check came back against me. I upsized this leg on the argument that compressed contango had reduced the roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry. Measuring it now: VIXM/VIXY rose +3.9% over five sessions against a ~1.1%/week average across the prior three months, and after netting each fund's beta to spot (VIXY ~0.87, VIXM ~0.45) that leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. The carry advantage I paid up for has not merely faded, it has inverted, and the leg is -9.4% on the month as a result. The value case thinned in parallel and not in the way I expected: VIX at 14.25 against 10d realized of 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium - near a normal risk premium, not a cheap one - and it got there because realized vol fell faster than implied, with 10d 11.64 below 20d 13.33 below 60d 13.93. I am cutting rather than exiting because the reasons to hold insurance are still genuinely present and cheap on the axes that matter for convexity: VVIX at 87.48 means options on VIX itself are near the low end of their range, SKEW rose 4.4% to 138.36 during a week ATM vol fell 4.4% so someone is quietly bidding tails, VIX sits at the 2nd percentile of its trailing year, and the 15-16 September FOMC is a dated binary inside my horizon now carrying an active energy-inflation impulse. This leg was positive by +5.8% to +12.4% on every one of SPY's eight worst days of the year; nothing else I own is convex like that. So it stays, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position, funded partly into XLE which expresses the same shock at positive carry. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that has never changed: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

reassessment_note:
Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.
novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the novelty against my own prior book is that I have replaced a paid-for-defensiveness structure (min-vol and low-vol funds that buy calm with surrendered return, plus a front-month vol ETF paying ~50%/yr to carry) with an earned-defensiveness structure - equal-weight index beta that gets its low volatility free from record dispersion, and an energy leg that has historically been positive on the days the index falls hardest - cutting the bleeding hedge to true tail size rather than treating insurance as a position.
research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED BEFORE I COULD USE IT (200/200 consumed at session start), so this week's work is built entirely on price/vol data I pulled and computed myself from the Yahoo chart API through the 2026-08-14 close, plus one FedWatch fetch that returned no probabilities. Stooq and Cboe's delayed-quote CDN both blocked me. All numbers below are my own calculations.

VOL STATE. VIX closed 14.25, down from 15.15 at my 08-10 entry and a new low for this experiment, 2nd percentile of the trailing year (1y range 13.47-31.05). SPY realized: 10d 11.64%, 20d 13.33%, 60d 13.93% - realized is DECELERATING, not reverting. This matters for my thesis: I underwrote long vol on "1.7 points of premium vs a 3-4 point norm" using 20d realized. Against 10d realized the premium is now 2.6 points, i.e. approaching normal. My edge did not close because VIX rose; it closed because realized fell faster than VIX did. VVIX 87.48 (cheap vol-of-vol) and SKEW 138.36, up +4.4% in a week VIX fell -4.4% - tail demand rising while ATM cheapens.

CARRY DETERIORATED, MEASURED. VIXM/VIXY rose from 0.7336 to 0.7622 in five sessions, +3.9% in a week against a ~1.1%/week average over the prior three months. Decomposing: VIX -4.4%, VIXY -4.8% (beta ~0.87 implies ~3.8% expected), VIXM -1.0% (beta ~0.45 implies ~2.0% expected). That is roughly 1 point per week of EXCESS front-month decay, ~50%/yr annualised. On 08-08 I wrote that compressed contango meant I was paying "a third to a half of the 43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry." That is no longer true - the roll cost is back at or above where I started. My single largest stated objection to this leg has re-armed.

DISPERSION IS STILL EXTREME AND I WAS EXPRESSING IT WRONG. SPY 20d rv 13.33 vs QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39 - the gap is intact. But RSP (equal-weight S&P) realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33/13.93. The equal-weighted index realizes ~27% LESS vol than the cap-weighted one. That falsifies the specific mechanism I used to justify a 40% SPY core: I invoked "index variance = average constituent variance x correlation" to argue the wrapper is safer than its contents at record-low correlation. That identity assumes equal weighting. In a cap-weighted index with ~40% in megacaps realizing 25-45%, concentration eats most of the correlation benefit - and RSP is the empirical proof, same tape, same window.

I STRESS-TESTED IT RATHER THAN TRUSTING 20 DAYS. Over SPY's 8 worst days of the trailing year, RSP's average downside capture is ~68%. Trailing 1y: RSP +21.8% vs SPY +22.0% - identical return - with max drawdown -7.9% vs -8.9%. RSP dominates SPY on every risk-adjusted measure I can compute, at 20d, 60d and 1y horizons.

ENERGY SHOCK, IGNORED BY EQUITIES. The single largest move in the tape: BNO (Brent) +7.9% on the week, USO +7.3%, XLE +7.7%, DBC +3.8% - the stalled Hormuz transit-fee negotiation I flagged on 08-08 evidently did not resolve. Meanwhile SPY +0.4% and VIX FELL. OVX dropped -11.3% on an +8% oil rally, so oil options read this as physical tightness rather than crisis. Rates confirm the inflation channel: ^IRX 3.70, unchanged on the month (front end pricing NO extra Fed), while ^TNX rose to 4.70, +2.8% on the month. A steepening driven by the long end with an anchored front end is a term-premium/inflation-expectations move, not a policy move.

HEDGE-QUALITY COMPARISON THAT DECIDED THE BOOK. On SPY's 8 worst days: XLE printed POSITIVE on 5 of 8; SPLV positive on 4 of 8; USMV ~60% capture on all 8; VIXY +5.8% to +12.4% on all 8. Trailing 1y return for that protection: XLE +49.2%, USMV +9.8%, SPLV +6.2%, VIXY -50.9%. XLE buys me drawdown protection at least as good as SPLV's while having returned eight times as much, and it is long the live macro shock instead of short it. SPLV, by contrast, is -0.57% over the month, is ~25% utilities against a 10y at 4.70 and rising, and its whole defensive premise is a rate call that the energy impulse is actively arguing against. XLU -2.55% on the month says the same thing.

SYNTHESIS. My vol sleeve is expensive insurance against a shock whose most likely proximate cause is sitting in plain sight in the oil tape. Owning the beneficiary of that shock is cheaper insurance than paying ~50%/yr to own the volatility it would create - so I fund most of the VIXY cut with XLE and keep VIXY only at genuine tail-hedge size into the dated 15-16 Sep FOMC.
